title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 10: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
keywords: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6) -- CJP's October 24, 2010 Inquirer column on how President Aquino can prevail in the 'crucial cases' before the Supreme Court -- the only body that 'can scuttle' his anti-corruption and anti-poverty programs because it answers to 'the Constitution and the rule of law,' not election promises

The four crucial cases discussed with presidential allies -- the Ombudsman's impeachment, the Truth Commission's constitutionality, the validity of midnight appointments, and the legality of public-private partnerships (PPP) -- and the two status quo ante (SQA) orders already issued

What SQA orders mean -- worded 'more benignly' than TROs to spare co-equal branches but with the same immediate effect, and signaling that the Court found the petitions 'prima facie meritorious,' so the government must 'rebut' that case to win, as it did in the SLEX matter

How cases are decided -- the 'analytical' formula (facts × law = decision) and the 'sociological' one (personality × stimuli = decision) -- and the counsel that P-Noy must persuade 'patiently and properly,' not by 'frontal criticisms,' remembering that 'the law is what the Supreme Court says it is'
sub_topics: The Court as the decisive obstacle: if anything 'can scuttle the avowed anti-corruption and anti-poverty programs' of Aquino, 'it is the Supreme Court' -- 'independent and apolitical,' bound not to 'election promises' but to the Constitution and rule of law that, per CJ Corona, 'will never bend to the ever-shifting political winds'

The crucial cases: in a 'tête-à-tête with presidential allies' (Drilon, Purisima, Abad, Soliman, Bautista, Santos, Cruz), CJP discussed 'the impeachment of the Ombudsman, the... Truth Commission, the validity of midnight appointments, and the legality of public-private partnerships (PPP)'

The SQA orders: the Court had issued two -- one barring the House Committee on Justice from hearing the impeachment complaints against Ombudsman Gutierrez, the other stopping the firing of alleged 'midnight appointee' Bai Omera Dianalan Lucman -- plus an earlier TRO halting the SLEX toll increases

SQA vs. TRO: status quo ante orders are 'worded more benignly than TROs so as not to offend co-equal branches,' but 'have the same effect,' taking effect immediately because, unlike TROs, they 'do not mandate the filing of bonds'

Prima facie meritorious: while SQAs and TROs 'do not necessarily guarantee the success of the petitioners,' their issuance 'implies that the Court has found the petitions to be prima facie meritorious,' so the respondents (the House and the Aquino administration) 'must rebut the prima facie case... to win'

The SLEX example: convinced by the respondents, the Court lifted the SLEX TRO and, in Francisco v. Toll Regulatory Board (Oct. 19, 2010), 'unanimously upheld' the PPP for the SLEX, NLEX and South Metro Manila Skyway -- Justice Velasco framing PPP as a viable strategy balancing 'the paramount common good for infrastructure projects' with 'a reasonable rate of return' to private investors, answering the ADB's call (via country director Neeraz Jain) that 'the judicial system will uphold contractual rights'

Two theories of judging: the 'analytical method' (the 'most commonly accepted'), where 'facts times law equals decision' (F × L = D) -- though 'many ways of interpreting... the law' leave it sometimes unable to predict the outcome; and the 'sociological school,' where 'personality times stimuli equals decision' (P × S = D), the magistrate's 'upbringing, education... religious faith, character... motivations' interacting with externals like 'public opinion, peer pressure... appointing authority'

The counsel: to win his cases, P-Noy must 'strategize patiently and properly,' using 'analytical and sociological ways of persuasion' rather than 'frontal criticisms,' and remembering that 'in the end, the law is what the Supreme Court says it is'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's October 24, 2010 Inquirer column, lays out how President Aquino can prevail in the 'crucial cases' before the Supreme Court -- the one body that 'can scuttle' his anti-corruption and anti-poverty programs because it is 'independent and apolitical' and bound to 'the Constitution and the rule of law,' which, per CJ Corona, 'will never bend to the ever-shifting political winds.' In a 'tête-à-tête' with presidential allies (Drilon, Purisima, Abad, Soliman, Bautista, Santos, Cruz), CJP had discussed four cases: 'the impeachment of the Ombudsman, the... Truth Commission, the validity of midnight appointments, and the legality of public-private partnerships (PPP).' The Court had issued two status quo ante (SQA) orders -- barring the House from hearing the Gutierrez impeachment, and stopping the firing of alleged 'midnight appointee' Bai Omera Dianalan Lucman -- plus an earlier SLEX TRO. SQAs, he explains, are 'worded more benignly than TROs' to spare co-equal branches but 'have the same effect,' biting immediately because they need no bonds; and their issuance 'implies that the Court has found the petitions to be prima facie meritorious,' so the respondents (the House and the administration) 'must rebut the prima facie case... to win.' That is what happened in the SLEX matter: persuaded by the respondents, the Court lifted the TRO and, in Francisco v. Toll Regulatory Board (2010), 'unanimously upheld' the SLEX/NLEX/Skyway PPPs -- Justice Velasco balancing 'the paramount common good for infrastructure' with 'a reasonable rate of return' to investors, and answering the ADB's call that 'the judicial system will uphold contractual rights.' Finally, CJP offers two models of how cases are decided -- the 'analytical' (facts × law = decision) and the 'sociological' (personality × stimuli = decision) -- and counsels that P-Noy must 'strategize patiently and properly,' using 'persuasion' rather than 'frontal criticisms,' remembering that 'in the end, the law is what the Supreme Court says it is.'
